Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The Fresh York Times reports.
  • Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.
  • According to recent reports, the year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The Fresh York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

According to recent reports, the year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave, but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Recent findings suggest that because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish fresh security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well.".

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

Sources indicate that their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

It has been revealed that in the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

According to recent reports, in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aston Villa were expecting some teething problems in 2026/27, but not being able to rely on home wins keeping them on track probably wasn’t one of them.

Recent findings suggest that villa seldom looked capable of breaking the deadlock in Saturday’s goalless draw with Sunderland. Their 2-1 win over Manchester City was their only home win in the Premier League in six attempts this season.

It’s a far cry from the general shape of Villa’s home from since Unai Emery took over as manager in the autumn of 2022. Villa Park has been the bedrock of the Emery revolution, but it’s anything but impenetrable so far this term.

Last season ended in triumph both in the fight for Champions League places and in the Europa League, but Villa’s faltering home form dates back to the start of 2026.

They won their first home match after the turn of the year but they lost their first home match for nearly four months when Everton visited Birmingham and won 1-0 in the middle of January. It was the same result against Brentford in the next home fixture and the aura, suddenly, was weakened.

A spate of midfield injuries affected those matches but Villa’s home form since Fresh Year’s Day includes as many losses as wins in the league – six of each – and failures this season to beat Nottingham Forest (now 17th in the table), Fulham (15th) and Sunderland (19th).

Whatever that indicates about why Villa might be struggling at home, it’s clearly a problem and Emery, while positive about aspects of Villa’s play against the Black Cats, isn’t shying away from that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It has been revealed that one place where his team don’t come up against the exact challenges posed by some of their Premier League opponents is in the Champions League, where Villa have won two home games out of two in the league phase this season. Indeed, European competitions underpin the very notion of Villa Park as a fortress under Emery, who took Villa back into Europe ahead of the 2023/24 season.

In a recent development, their last home loss in Europe was against Olympiacos in that year’s Conference League semi-finals. They won five out of six at home in the Champions League the next season, drawing the other, and won all seven of their home matches in their successful Europa League campaign in 2025/26.

While the idea of Villa being strong at home has endured, the evidence of it in the Premier League has not.

Sources indicate that villa’s home results in the league might have been short of their expected levels since before the summer, but there are differences between this season and last. Simply selling Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Emiliano Martinez, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Ollie Watkins fundamentally changed the picture at Villa Park.

According to recent reports, rogers and Tielemans were notable players for breaking games open. Villa significantly outscored their expected goals value in periods of last season and goals from outside the penalty area were key.

They don’t have the same superpower this season; improving their chance creation is a must and that’s not quick or easy with any group of players, never mind a newly assembled and young team.

While the idea of Villa being strong at home has endured, the evidence of it in the Premier League has not.

There’s also a looming, inconvenient possibility that’s beginning to sustain the weight of truth. Villa Park is a three-sided stadium this season because the North Stand – ordinarily full of home supporters – is being redeveloped behind one of the goals.

Sources indicate that the difference is intangible, indefinable, but it’s there. Even the players can’t quantify it because half of them have never played at a four-sided Villa Park, but the vacant structure behind the goal makes for an unusual atmosphere.

Industry observers note that emery has no interest in excuses. The Villa manager is focused on process and progress, taking every challenge for what it is and finding the answers to the questions they pose.

In a recent development, the North Stand redevelopment won’t be accepted as mitigation for poor home form in the dugout any more than it will in the other three stands, but Emery is no fool. He accepted after the Sunderland draw that Villa Park and the team who call it home are missing ‘something’ without the North Stand. It’s not an excuse, just another test.

Villa need to pass that test. Home results have been a hallmark of the Emery era. The manager himself has qualified for Europe every season since long before he succeeded Steven Gerrard.

It has been revealed that one win in six is a long way short of that standard. Emery’s meticulous and measured problem-solving has been called into action once more.

Chris is a Warwickshire-based freelance football writer specialising in West Midlands football, the Premier League, the EFL and the J.League. He is the author of the High Protein Beef Paste football newsletter and owner of Aston Villa Review. He supports Coventry Sphinx.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United are under new management and need to be under new leadership on the field.

In a recent development, bruno Fernandes has undeniably been a flickering beacon of brief hope for United in darkening times. He’s been their Player of the Year in five of the last seven seasons, risen to 19th of their greatest scorers with 113 goals, has scored 75 times (24 pens, four free-kicks) and provided 74 assists in 240 Premier League games and is the reigning Footballer of the Year. But it’s undeniably time for the club to face reality, resist the urge to extend a contract which expires next summer and build for the future.

Sources indicate that even taking up the year’s option (unless to increase the player’s transfer fee) would be a retrograde step. Fernandes is 32, slowing up, and not now “best in class, 10 out of 10s” to borrow Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s catchphrase. He is not the most convincing of captains, moans too much and flaps his arms like a fledgling dove attempting to leave the nest.

Fernandes would never, ever be considered one of United’s elite captains in a strong, historic field that includes Sir Bobby Charlton, Roy Keane, Bryan Robson, Steve Bruce, Roger Byrne, Nemanja Vidic and Gary Neville, amongst others.

All are different; Neville was very vocal, Charlton led by example, but were united in their total commitment.

Sources indicate that fernandes’ leadership qualities were brought into question when he openly criticised the tactics of Michael Carrick, effectively undermining him. That may not have been Fernandes’ intention when questioning the tactical approach against Como but it certainly didn’t help Carrick at a time when he needed players standing up to be counted, not standing up to his tactics in public. Such concerns – some of them legitimate – should have been aired in private.

It has been revealed that it highlighted a lack of leadership from Fernandes, a lack of gratitude, too. Fernandes wouldn’t have been named the writers’ Footballer of the Year and the players’ Player of the Year without Carrick reviving United’s fortunes and their No. 8’s form last season.

Breaking: NWSL, U.S. Soccer continue focus on women's soccer growth with player and executive development programs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that WASHINGTON, D.C.
  • Sources indicate that in the first of four announcements she teased was in service of that.
  • The NWSL's new initiatives reflect a shifting focus across the American soccer landscape, one that seems driven by the heightened interest in the sport courtesy of this year's World Cup in North America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that WASHINGTON, D.C. – The NWSL has always been a measuring stick for the growth of women's soccer in the U.S., which in recent years has been headlined by skyrocketing expansion fees and increased fan engagement. There's a buzzword that continues to pop up around the league, one that is rarely associated with the key performance indicators – pipeline. After she read out another list of attendance figures and viewership numbers before the 2026 season wraps up with Saturday's NWSL Championship (8 p.m. ET, CBS, Paramount+), commissioner Jessica Berman made a hard pivot in her state of the league remarks on Thursday to say the league is officially in the business of prioritizing said pipeline.

Sources indicate that in the first of four announcements she teased was in service of that. The NWSL announced two initiatives on Thursday: the creation of a player development rule (PDR) and a sporting executive leadership program, designed specifically to focus on the foundation of the league's structure. The plans are a marriage of the league's business model and sporting objectives, a tacit understanding that the two go hand-in-hand, especially for a league that is admittedly driven by star power. These new plans, though, are hardly the only initiatives that will influence the pipeline.

The NWSL's new initiatives reflect a shifting focus across the American soccer landscape, one that seems driven by the heightened interest in the sport courtesy of this year's World Cup in North America. The league's financial stability enabled this shift but beyond that, there are overlapping commitments across the industry to finally fix one of American soccer's most evident problems – the pipeline. The sport's success in this country has often come in spite of a fractured youth soccer system, one that U.S. Soccer hopes to unite in the coming years.

The parties, be it in conjunction or individually, are also dead set on ensuring the women's game is held in equal regard to the men's every step of the way.

In a recent development, the PDR joins a list of NWSL rules in recent years that have incentivized clubs to recruit young players more easily such as the U-18 Entry Mechanism and organizing its first-ever combine last year. The new rule requires participating clubs to develop a curriculum that supports player development and is tied directly to salary cap relief.

According to recent reports, "What can we do at the league to motivate and incentivize clubs to develop players?" Sarah Gregorius, the NWSL's vice president of sporting, told CBS Sports. "What do we have in our toolkit? And one of the things we obviously have in our toolkit is a salary cap and we can use that as a motivation and as an incentive to encourage the types of behavior around player development that we want to see, and hopefully, it's really our first structural foray into player development. Again, it's deliberately an incentive. It's not a mandate. It's up to the clubs. If they want to participate, if they want to access the reward, they know what they have to do in order to do that.".

Recent findings suggest that there is a perceived industry standard about developing young players, even if it is as far from an exact science as it gets. Academy systems tied to clubs are how players often come up the ranks – that is true across the men's game including in MLS and increasingly so for women's players in Europe. The NWSL does not have a streamlined system that mirrors the academy set-up and interestingly enough, is not actually trying to go in that direction.

In a recent development, "This is a pretty unique country," Gregorius noted. "It doesn't actually work to pick something up from overseas and plop it down over here and I'm actually not convinced in the two years that I've spent here and everything that I've learned that this vertical academy system across the clubs makes the most sense. There's already a ton of incredible player development happening. There's just a bit of a lack of cohesion and a lack of connection to the professional game … The Spanish model won't work here, the German model wouldn't work here, the Japanese model wouldn't work here. Got a ton of respect for what they're doing in their countries but the reason that it works is it's for those countries. We have to do something that works for this one, which has characteristics that no other country in the world has. F---, this place is big. It's dynamic. There's a lot going on.".

Gregorius believes a league-issued mandate might further fracture an already splintered landscape.

"If I think about it from a local level, some of our clubs are in markets that have thriving youth ecosystems, right?" Gregorius started. "So if all of a sudden there was a mandate from the league that every single club – which is what they do in England – has to come in and have a professional game academy, they're going to all of a sudden have to start pulling players out of those environments, which is disruptive for the kids. It's disruptive for the families. Some of those kids and families are also fans of the team. It's the icing on the cake in those particular markets so all of a sudden, you create tension. You create tension for the parents. You create tension for the kids. You create tension within the fan groups. They're like, 'Well, no, actually. You've stripped out my youth club in order to service a mandate from the league, not paying attention to the fact that all of your talented players have come through the system.' That's not what we want. That's bad for player development and it's bad for fan engagement, to be honest.".

The NWSL is distinguishing itself from MLS, a league to which it has no formal ties but one that committed to the traditional academy system over a decade ago and can count it amongst its greatest successes. There's no stigma associated with the diverging path, though – U.S. Soccer has committed to viewing the women's game specifically through a female lens in recent years, an initiative championed by U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes but embraced by many, either through her influence or separate from it.

"The intense focus on the pathway is very intentional," U.S. Soccer COO Dan Helfrich told CBS Sports. "The intense focus as we build the next version of the women and girls pathway, that it's done through a female lens, is very intentional and look, there is going to be, we believe, historic investment and interest in women's soccer and it's it's going to crescendo into the 2031 World Cup and making sure we take advantage of this moment to corral and direct the investment and interest in a sustainable way. I don't think there's anything that could have a greater legacy for women's soccer in our country than that.".

The distinction between the men's and women's games, even at the youth levels, is easy for Helfrich to make because they have always existed.

Industry observers note that "The first thing is the environments for players to develop in," he noted. "it's really crucial that they're tailored to women and girl  and that includes environments for youth clubs and colleges and professional clubs and so some of the work, for example, of the Kang Women's Institute becomes really important to do the research to develop the insights and then for us to promulgate them into all these areas, that's different and if you look at the as-is state of the pathway, the league structures for girls are different than the league structures for boys. The role of college soccer for girls is different than the role of college soccer for boys and so practically, if you're trying to optimize a future, you apply a different lens.".

Recent findings suggest that there's more shared consensus when it comes to developing leaders that will foster players' growth, which is where the sporting executive leadership program kicks in. The program is built around specialized education for sporting director types, the first yearlong edition of the initiative already in session. A cohort of six – Haley Carter of the Washington Spirit, Caitlin Carducci of the Orlando Pride, Angela Mangano of the Houston Dash, Jeff Agoos of the Portland Thorns, Kelly Cousins of the Utah Royals and Dome Guasch of the Boston Legacy – already took part in their first session of a project supported both by U.S. Soccer and FIFA.

"The 16, now 18, individuals who hold the highest sporting position at the clubs have an outsized impact on the on-field identity and on-field product of their club so therefore, all of those people have an an impact on the on-field product of the league," Gregorius noted. "It's also, curiously enough, one of the few roles within the sporting department that doesn't have a license. You don't need to have completed a particular license. There's no education requirements or anything like that so when we also did an audit of the 16 clubs and who was holding those positions, some have former players, some have lawyers, some have people with an operations background, some have people with a coaching background. It was very varied so we're like, okay, if we know that this group has a ton of impact, if we know that they don't go through any structured learning. Is there a way that we can wrap our arms around them and support them?".

The uniqueness of this program is that it is tied specifically to the NWSL, which operates independently of a men's league unlike some of its European counterparts or even the WNBA.

"It's the first of its kind because every other f---ing part of the world just cares about men's football so we're really, really proud of not only the commitment and the discipline around trying to get it off the ground," Gregorius noted.

It is in parallel with other initiatives the league and U.S. Soccer have worked on in recent years. The NWSL combine, for example, was also an effort to bolster female coaches while U.S. Soccer frequently uses its new national training center to conduct coaching courses with the youth game in mind.

"What I would say is to grow the game the way it needs to be grown, we can't underestimate or overlook the non-player part of development," Helfrich said, "and the non-player part of development is coaches. The non-player part of development is scouts. Non-player part of development is referees and the non-player part of development is front office, technical leaders and so, building a partnership with the NWSL on all of those vital non-player development activities is a massive priority.".

Sources indicate that the NWSL's partnership with U.S. Soccer on this program also speaks to a unique truth about American soccer. The women's game is held in incredibly high regard in the U.S. because of the historic success of the USWNT, who have four World Cup titles and five Olympic gold medals in their 40-year history. The USWNT's reputation of being serial winners is intrinsically tied to the health of the federation, the NWSL and in some ways, American soccer as a whole.

Sources indicate that "Honest to God, I've loved waking up every day and only thinking about the women's game," Gregorius, a former Newly introduced Zealand international, mentioned. "It's brilliant and it's very unique over here that we are able to do that and what I love about working with U.S. Soccer, as well, to be honest, is they're the same. They're almost more interested in the women's game sometimes than they are anything else … It's an organization that is already on the train, you know what I mean? The NWSL and our clubs, it's not even a question of being in the shadow of the men's game or any of that other bulls--- that you kind of encounter in other places. The focus is unwavering and that's brilliant.".

Industry News: Hashim Thaci's second conviction in The Hague reignites debate in Kosovo about justice and the Kosovo Specialist Chambers

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.
  • This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.
  • According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his recent war crimes trial and sentenced him to 17 months in prison.

This term will be added to his 25-year sentence for war crimes, which was handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16.

According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility in The Hague with confidential information about witnesses in his war crimes trial and had instructed them on how to influence their testimony.

Three other men — former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu — were also convicted.

Thaci, who was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War, is viewed by many in his home country as a hero. His war crimes conviction in September was greeted in Kosovo with anger and dismay.

Thaci has vowed to appeal the war crimes conviction.

His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society. Tuesday's ruling brings renewed attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role played by its former leaders, and the continuing debate over justice, individual or collective responsibility for the KLA's war to liberate Kosovo from Serbia, and trust in judicial institutions.

The response from the government of Kosovo was swift.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, the government mentioned, "Trust in justice is built not only on the decisions that are made, but also on the manner in which they are reached. Therefore, our commitment to the rule of law and our insistence on the full respect of rights and procedural guarantees are part of the same principled position: Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible.".

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States.

The court was created to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by members of the KLA during and after the Kosovo War.

For security reasons, including concerns about witness intimidation, the court was located in The Hague in the Netherlands.

After Thaci and three others were convicted of war crimes in first instance in September, Kosovo's state authorities established a working group to draft a strategy regarding the appeal proceedings before the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The group is chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca and includes members of Kosovo's parliament.

Prime Minister Albin Kurti has stated that the working group continues to believe that "the first-instance judgment of the Specialist Chambers is unjust, both legally and morally," and that as a result, "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers.".

In addition, the parliament of Kosovo is at the moment considering amendments to the law governing the Kosovo Specialist Chambers.

The draft law, which is expected to be adopted, envisages narrowing the court's mandate in several areas, including the time period covered by its jurisdiction, limiting the maximum prison sentence to 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing the possibility of presidential pardons for persons convicted by final court decisions.

How do political analysts and legal experts view the parliament's attempt to amend the law on the Kosovo Specialist Chambers before the judicial process involving the four men convicted of war crimes has reached a final verdict?

"From an international perspective, at first glance, this initiative could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," stated political analyst and university professor Artan Muhaxheri.

"Precisely for this reason, it is essential that Kosovo's political spectrum and its legal experts demonstrate beyond any doubt that this measure does not conflict with Kosovo's international obligations toward the European Union," Muhaxheri told DW, adding that this is the only way to ensure that the desired outcome is achieved and that the initiative does not produce the opposite effect.

"Issues relating to jurisdiction, statutory limits on maximum sentences, and other similar matters must be argued professionally and rigorously, demonstrating that they fully guarantee judicial independence and enjoy solid support within Kosovo's legal system, the same legal system that, first and foremost, established the Specialist Chambers," he mentioned.

Ehat Miftaraj, executive director of the Kosovo Law Institute (IKD), told DW that although the Kosovo Specialist Chambers were established by the Republic of Kosovo itself, "the way the judicial process has unfolded has created the impression that judges, prosecutors and certain international actors have treated not only the accused but also Kosovo itself with distrust, prejudice, and an often condescending approach.".

Miftaraj went on to say that reactions and objections in Kosovo to the decisions of the Specialist Chambers are also interpreted and judged in the historical and emotional context of the war and what Kosovo's citizens experienced during and after it.

"In a democratic society, every citizen, including political and institutional representatives, has the right to criticize judicial decisions," he mentioned. "However, there is a fundamental distinction between criticism based on legal arguments and attempts to delegitimize courts or exert influence over judicial proceedings. And here, there is room for criticism of both sides.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the third straight time, the Washington Spirit are playing for the NWSL Championship.
  • According to recent reports, the Washington Spirit won it all in 2021 but came up just short in each of the last two finals.
  • The Kansas City Current bring plenty to the final and may just be the favorites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the third straight time, the Washington Spirit are playing for the NWSL Championship. The No. 3 Spirit host the No. 4 Kansas City Current at Audi Field on Saturday for the biggest prize in domestic women's soccer. Kickoff is at 8 p.m. ET, and you can see it all on CBS and Paramount+.

According to recent reports, the Washington Spirit won it all in 2021 but came up just short in each of the last two finals. This may be the day that Trinity Rodman gets her second crown.

The Kansas City Current bring plenty to the final and may just be the favorites. They're back in the major game for the first time since 2022 after ending NJ/NY Gotham FC's title defense in the semis. Croix Bethune, who used to play for the Spirit, curled in a free-kick stunner, and Haley Hopkins won it in the 89th minute.

So who lifts the trophy? Our experts make their picks below.

Industry observers note that star-studded attack: This year's finalists did not have the most straightforward journeys to the NWSL Championship, but the good news for each of them is that there will be few excuses when they finally take to the pitch on Saturday. Trinity Rodman is about to cap off a career-best campaign after an injury-riddled 2025 season and will be joined by the impactful Sofia Cantore and midseason arrival Clara Luvanga, putting the Washington Spirit in as good a position as any to come out with a win that has eluded them over the last two seasons. The Current, though, are in the same boat --  they have struggled without their all-star trio, but each of Croix Bethune, Temwa Chawinga and Michelle Cooper will be available on Saturday and equally capable of turning the game in their favor.

Sources indicate that midfield battles: There's going to be a real display of veteran prowess and eager energy. Both teams have experienced players and rising stars, and it'll be a combo of chess and tug of war during the NWSL Championship. Washington Spirit's Andi Sullivan anchors most things in the middle, with Leicy Santos linking play and Melissa Bethi's recent rise in form. Even with all the changes from injuries to departures and returns from maternity leave, the Spirit are gelling at a good time in a crucial part of the pitch. They'll battle against Kansas City's Lo'eau LaBonta and Vanessa DiBernardo, two of the best in the league with longevity and finesse. Ball knowers understand that they're two players who can control a game, close and create lanes, or serve up goals and assists. Add attacking mid Croix Bethune into the mix, and Kansas City have plenty of ways to win the middle of the park. -- Sandra Herrera.

Balance: At their best, the Washington Spirit are a side who can win a game in multiple ways, and while there's plenty of star power on both sides, balance is where they win out. It's a fascinating match for both sides and one where the margins will be thin but being able to have a strong attack led by Trinity Rodman along with a buildup that Andi Sullivan keeps control of. If the Spirit can control the pace, it will be a long day for Kansas City but Croix Bethune will have ideas of her own as well. -- Chuck Booth.

Sources indicate that washington Spirit: The Spirit have tossed around the phrase that the third time's the charm after two empty-handed trips to the NWSL Championship and this year, it's hard not to buy the argument. Rodman is happy and healthy but she is just one part of a team that has been smartly assembled over the years and seems as cohesive as ever. -- Pardeep Cattry.

Washington Spirit: Truthfully, the pressure is on the Washington Spirit headed into this one, and that typically doesn't play out the best for teams who are the higher seed or considered favorites on paper. Kansas City will be a more than worthy opponent, but the Spirit's third time in the final comes with a long home build-up through and back to Audi Field, and any mental component needed will come with a boost from the crowd environment. -- Sandra Herrera.

Washington Spirit: Sure, this is a "neutral" venue, but being a home team in a final match will carry the Spirit at Rowdy Audi. Considering that this is the third consecutive final, fans snatched up tickets as soon as they could, assuming that the home side would be here. While all the pressure is on the Spirit and rightfully so, the team has also embraced that, and once the first goal goes in the net, this is going to turn into a party. -- Chuck Booth.

Trinity Rodman: Is this an obvious choice? Yes, yes it is, but to be fair, Rodman has earned the right to be the easy pick. She has always been key to the Spirit's success but hit a new level this season, to the point that she had a very valid MVP case even if her ex-teammate Ashley Sanchez took it home instead after a record-breaking season with the North Carolina Courage. Rodman's ability to create and score chances means she's very likely to have a say on Saturday, one that could very well end the Spirit's five-year wait for another championship. -- Pardeep Cattry.

Sources indicate that clara Luvanga: The last few NWSL Championship MVPs have gone to the lone goal scorer. Barbra Banda won it in 2024 for her game-winning goal, and Rose Lavelle earned it for her single title goal in 2025. If these two teams match up on the pitch as evenly as they do on paper, then it could come down to a single moment again, and Luvanga has shown she's better positioned for it with her current form. Her four goals and three assists through seven games make her an efficient threat on goal, and could finally be the difference maker for the group in their third final. -- Sandra Herrera.

In a recent development, trinity Rodman: To win finals, you need your best players to be at their best. All eyes have been on Trinity Rodman this season after she became the highest-paid player in NWSL history, and she has delivered. Considering that the next development in her career is to become a player for the biggest moments, and capping off the final by scoring will be just the way to do it. -- Chuck Booth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 17:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:02 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • Sources indicate that the message from Enzo Maresca ought to be clear when Manchester City convene for their meeting at the training ground this weekend before heading down to London.
  • Recent findings suggest that he has to say that Arsenal away must be considered the perfect game for his players at this point.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Published: 17:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:02 EST, 25 November 2026.

Sources indicate that the message from Enzo Maresca ought to be clear when Manchester City convene for their meeting at the training ground this weekend before heading down to London. Clear because there is no other appropriate message to impart, really.

Recent findings suggest that he has to say that Arsenal away must be considered the perfect game for his players at this point. The opportunity to reignite their season, to stand up, to show the Premier League they are not going anywhere just quite yet. Squads who went before them would certainly approach a fixture of this magnitude with that attitude. A squad with Kevin De Bruyne as its linchpin would.

City were still searching for answers against Napoli, a point rescued late on by Rayan Cherki. But despite the growing frustration in the stands, that unmistakable guttural desperation for just a bit more of something, it was better. More joined up thinking, at least.

Recent findings suggest that an inverted full back did that for them and it perhaps should be the blueprint for the manager when they arrive at the Emirates on Sunday. City were eminently more comfortable with that; knew where they stood. Nico O'Reilly was not particularly brilliant in that position yet his presence, the safety net of somebody alongside Ayyoub Bouaddi in possession and in turn freeing up Elliot Anderson will surely make City more formidable as the weeks go by.

According to recent reports, the set-up presented another tactical tweak for Maresca as he searches for answers and consistency. Defensively, City were twice undone by individual mistakes rather than the overarching plan, one that stifled the enduring class of De Bruyne.

A gentle hum, the half-hearted chants for a returning king, resembled an afternoon session in front of a crowd drowsy from their liquid lunches before a seesawing four-goal second half felt more befitting of City's guest for the evening, UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin – intriguingly entertained by chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak in the directors' box.

Rayan Cherki rescued a point late on but this was another difficult night for Man City.

Former Man United striker Rasmus Hojlund celebrates his goal against his old rivals.

Ayyoub Bouaddi scored his first goal for Manchester City since joining from Lille.

It has been revealed that city, sporting a fourth kit that had an unfortunate Guantanamo quality to it, certainly had more of a clue than they did here on Saturday. There were clearer patterns – noticeably Marc Guehi piercing midfield lines with one incisive pass for O'Reilly – but this is a team whose confidence has been shaken in recent weeks and that will not return overnight. 'We were aggressive off the ball,' remarked Maresca, while bemoaning conceding for a tenth consecutive match. 'Defensively we were good, pressing good.'.

In a recent development, regardless, City's supporters definitely demanded more caution thrown to the wind and some of their players wore those looks too. Anderson's dangerous crosses from that right-hand channel – the area presided over by De Bruyne for a decade – occasionally proved unsettling for Napoli, while Allan should have scored from a ricocheting corner as captain Erling Haaland claimed a penalty for being dragged down.

Man City (4-2-3-1): Donnarumma 6; Nunes 5, Guehi 5, Gvardiol 6, O'Reilly 5; Bouaddi 7, Anderson 6; Cherki 7, Fernandez 6 (Ndiaye 63, 6), Allan 5 (Doku 54, 7); Haaland 5.

Napoli (4-1-4-1): Milinkovic-Savic 6; Spinazzola 7, Beukema 6, Rrahmani 7, Olivera 6; Gilmour 8; Politano 6, McTominay 6, De Bruyne 6, Lang 7; Hojlund 7.

Manager: Massimiliano Allegri 7.

In a sign that Maresca was placing more players in threatening areas, O'Reilly had headed over a Matheus Nunes cross – yet chances had been at a premium, those who should be protagonists taking too many safe options rather than pushing chests out and relishing responsibility.

In a recent development, and when there was risk, Napoli pounced. Cherki the culprit, flicking a ball around the corner aimlessly into the middle of his own half. Billy Gilmour gave thanks, punched towards Rasmus Hojlund and he spun Guehi to flash under Donnarumma ten minutes into the second half. Hojlund celebrated by shouting 'one club in Manchester' while holding a single finger aloft. 'It's good banter,' he said and we'll take his word for that.

City had been warned of the danger, when Noa Lang went clean through before checking back upon realising he didn't possess the acceleration to complete the job.

Maresca's assistant, Danny Walker, shook his head on the bench as they pored over the goal's replay. Enzo Fernandez was planting his boot into one of Vanja Milinkovic-Savic's posts when the goalkeeper nonchalantly plucked a floated cross from the night sky.

City had stirred somewhat though, helped by the inclusion of Jeremy Doku – ironically introduced seconds before Hojlund's opener – and it was the Belgian who made their equaliser seven minutes after the hour. He waited and waited inside Napoli's box for defenders to commit, finding Bouaddi alone and the teenager wrapped his left foot around the pass and was quickly racing back to halfway.

There had appeared a head of steam, only for O'Reilly to be caught well out of position as Napoli countered – City carved open – and Lang thundered a volley past Donnarumma with 14 minutes left. Cherki made amends for his earlier error by hammering into the far corner but was less than pleased.

In a recent development, 'We played good but we don't give a lot of energy,' Cherki noted. 'We need to do more, we need to win these games, and today I don't care (about) scoring my goal. I want to win this game. We're going to London to win.'.

In fact, maybe that is the team talk.

In a recent development, michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Sources indicate that going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

Industry observers note that "Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP.

It has been revealed that did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

Recent findings suggest that united are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Recent findings suggest that chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

Recent findings suggest that but analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

Sources indicate that but, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once noted. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the significant question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

In a recent development, with four Premier League games in progress the picture is ever-changing, but United are right now 19th in the Premier League table. The club, famously, were relegated in 1974 with the coup de grâce applied by Denis Law’s backheel when the Scot was playing in a City shirt. In this piece, James Ducker looks back on the previous occasions when one of the world’s biggest clubs has flirted with calamity.

When Villa dropped into the Championship, it did not change the fact they were the biggest club in the Midlands. No matter what Tom Brady does at Birmingham City, that’s not changing any time soon. They sought and achieved promotion by raiding Brentford.

Nobody was complaining about a sleeping giant taking Dean Smith, Ezri Konsa or Ollie Watkins and potentially stalling Brentford’s progression.

Nor was it suggested hiring Emery from Villarreal was an odd move given that the Spanish side had recently won the Europa League and reached the latter stages of the Champions League.

Michael Carrick states he has been given no assurances about his future beyond this afternoon’s crucial game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.United are searching for only their second Premier League win of the season and first in 70 days after the club’s worst start to a campaign for 40 years piled the pressure on Carrick.They dropped into the relegation zone last night following Nottingham Forest’s victory over Manchester City and will be bottom by the end of the weekend if they lose to Villa and Crystal Palace and Sunderland both win.The Old Trafford hierarchy opted to give Carrick more time to try to turn their season around following a 3-0 hammering by Bournemouth and 4-1 drubbing in Como, since when United have been beaten 2-0 by Chelsea and recovered from two goals down to overcome Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday night.Asked if he had been told outright he would still be in charge next week, Carrick said: “No - no. Just carry on as absolute normal.”Pressed on when he felt his future was uncertain, the head coach added: “No, no. Whatever happens and what’s going to happen is going to happen in terms of the game, we’ve got to prepare right.“I’m really looking forward to playing at home on the back of the other night. The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming and energised and feeling good about what they might see and we’ve got to repay that.”Another defeat would leave the United board with a big decision to make around Carrick’s future at a time when they are under severe attack from the fanbase.United’s game against Roma was briefly interrupted when tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch in the first half of a game notable for more furious protests against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.Three people were arrested by Greater Manchester Police for throwing items on to the pitch and are understood to have been hit with automatic three-year football banning orders as a consequence. More in-stadium demonstrations are expected today with regular match going fans encouraged not to buy alcohol or drinks inside Old Trafford and again release green and gold balloons before kick-off.Green and gold were the club’s original colours as Newton Heath and have become a symbol of protest against the ownership. Asked why there had been such a big drop-off from last season, Carrick added: “It’s just inconsistency, that’s within games,” he said.“It can be a number of things, it’s never just one thing: a bit of decision-making, a bit of concentration, things going against us in certain points, sometimes we haven’t helped ourselves. So there’s no excuses for it, it is what it is. The great thing is we can do something about it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bayern Munich's depth was already pushed to the limit, but Friday's 1-1 draw with Koln may have broken Vincent Kompany's side. Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane lasted only 20 minutes before exiting with what the club is calling a "syndesmosis ligament tear in his left ankle," which required surgery overnight and will keep him sidelined "for months," according to sporting director Max Eberl.

According to recent reports, "Harry Kane underwent successful surgery overnight after tearing his left ankle ligament in yesterday's home match against 1. FC Köln. The 33-year-old will now begin his rehab," Bayern remarked in a statement.

Counting down the days already ❤️‍🩹 pic.twitter.com/rpNWUxc4vW.

According to recent reports, losing Kane alone is a significant blow to the Bavarians after they failed to replace Nicolas Jackson when his loan ended, but the injuries didn't stop there. Michael Olise was also withdrawn at halftime and left the stadium on crutches.

It has been revealed that this led to a match in which Bayern put only one shot on target against a side just above the relegation zone, showing this is a problem of their own creation in the transfer market. Coming into the season without a viable backup for an aging Kane would eventually hurt Bayern, and Kompany now needs to oversee a worst-case scenario. Luis Diaz and Ismael Saibari were already out with injuries, and when Kane went down, Thomas Bischof had to come in for him instead of a like-for-like striker. Even with Jamal Musiala's neurological challenges, the players they do have aren't able to perform at their best.

Already in an actual title race in the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund, these are the kinds of setbacks that can lead to a new German champion for the first time since Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24, and even they had to go undefeated to accomplish that feat, while this season could be Bayern's own undoing. They've been one of the top sides in the world when healthy, but as it is, this side will struggle in Champions League play, where they'll travel to face Lille. Precariously in 13th place in the Champions League league phase, Bayern won't fall out of the top 24 without Kane, but it could get close to something that they should be concerned about. Even missing out on the top eight and needing to play additional games is something that Bayern won't want to deal with, considering this injury crisis.

Being a backup to Kane is a thankless task, as it's hard to get game time and you're also compared to one of the best players in the world, but it's still a multifaceted failure for Bayern to not have one. Real Madrid were able to recruit post-prime players to back up Karim Benzema, and now Kylian Mbappe has a backup from the academy. There's no reason that a club of Bayern's stature shouldn't be able to do the same, but here we are in the same position they constantly find themselves in.

It has been revealed that depth issues have held Bayern back from claiming a Champions League title in recent years. Kane winning the Ballon d'Or solidified that the starting XI is more than good enough to lift Europe's most coveted club trophy, and the difference between this side and the 2020 one that won the Champions League is their lack of depth.

It's a strange situation with Musiala that isn't being handled well, with board members open to selling him, and it doesn't help the club's overall trajectory. Bayern will need to shake things up in January, but these issues began long before now, and to return to the top of the global game, they need to change the way they do things.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“You’re not famous any more,” was one of the many taunts from The Kop aimed at Manchester United as Liverpool romped to a 4-0 win against Maurico Pochettino’s newly introduced team.

Industry observers note that of course, the early dismissal of Leny Yoro helped the home side and hindered their relegation zone opponents, but it’s hard to think the result would have been much different if this had been 11 vs. 11 throughout.

Liverpool finished the match having missed six big chances.

In a recent development, alexander Isak, who was highly impressive in the first half, especially, with his off-the-ball movement and defensive work seemingly improving under Andoni Iraola, had a goal-bound effort blocked by Harry Maguire before the break and blazed a good chance wide in the second half. On another day, the Swede would’ve bagged two.

Bradley Barcola, who is far from a clinical finisher, had several opportunities to score himself or assist another. His pace for the third goal indicates where his strengths are but his composure in front of goal is an area of weakness.

"Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more,” insisted Pochettino post-match.

According to recent reports, maybe he was right, because Liverpool were sensational going forward, their front four connecting superbly, with Florian Wirtz the chief orchestrator. The German is really finding form for Iraola’s side and created an incredible 10 chances in the game - five of them defined as massive chances.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That’s the most chances created by a single player in a Premier League game since 2015.

Then there was Rio Ngumoha, the teenager absolutely tormenting Diogo Dalot, and unsurprisingly, completing the most dribbles in the game and having the most touches in the opposition box.

Liverpool ended the game with 60 touches inside Manchester United’s box, 28 shots on goal, and an xG of 4.35 - which is vastly higher than recorded in the 7-0 mauling three years ago (2.91).

That this was the fifth time in five years that Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker had played a game between these sides and won by at least a three-goal margin underlines the chasm between the two north-west rivals.

It has been revealed that alisson has stood in the Liverpool goal for a 7-0, a 5-0, two 4-0s, and a 3-0 victory all since 2021. For Liverpool fans who sat through the nineties, and parts of the noughties, having their dreams shattered by Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United, this is an experience that heals many childhood traumas.

But, as much as the 1990s were a barren decade in Liverpool’s history, they were never as bad as this post-Ferguson United are.

In a recent development, in fact, Liverpool never lost to United by more than a two-goal margin throughout their worst decade in the modern era. A 4-0 reverse at Old Trafford in 2003 and a 3-0 in 2014 are the only two times United have beaten Liverpool by more than two goals since 1969.

In the last 50 years, United’s top scorer in this fixture is Marcus Rashford with seven goals. In that same time, Mo Salah scored 16 and Steven Gerrard nine.

Industry observers note that liverpool weren’t great during the ‘90s and for parts of the ‘00s, but they were at least competitive, especially in these fixtures that mean so much to supporters. United once again crumbled against their main rival, the two teams that have won the league title the joint-most times in English football history.

Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more.

Sources indicate that “Going down with the City,” was another chant from the Liverpool faithful, who enjoyed seeing Iraola give some Jurgen Klopp-like celebrations, albeit much less extravagant, post-match. “Always I enjoy the moment,” stated the Spaniard. “I think we owe them (the fans) because we have had much better results away and we want to solve this and want to give them a big win and more to celebrate.”This is a huge win for Iraola, whose Liverpool career has begun well but seen disappointing home results in his first five league games.

It has been revealed that with a big win over Man United now under his belt, the confidence is brimming. “I’m pretty sure things are going to be falling into place for the club,” remarked a buoyed Virgil van Dijk. “It takes a bit of time, when you are new at any profession or any place you work at you need a little bit of time.”.

Time is something United don’t have, with only one league win by late November and firmly in the relegation zone.

This game and the situation of both teams, each with upcoming managers but at different stages in their development, truly underlined how Liverpool have managed to avoid the post-Klopp era capitulation that United have been troubled by for the last 13 years.

One club had a successful manager oversee an era of dominance, the other is a successful club with multiple eras of dominance under different managers.

#117809. Leeds expose Chelsea's unresolved defensive problems as Xabi Alonso's crew yet to find footing

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1140 w)

Leeds expose Chelsea's unresolved defensive problems as Xabi Alonso's crew yet to find footing

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that LONDON -- This was supposed to be the year, the time when Chelsea grew up and a proper manager started extracting consistent performances from a squad whose much-vaunted talent is too rarely expressed in results form.
  • Recent findings suggest that once more, however, that is threatening to be a standard beyond Chelsea.
  • Industry observers note that and Alonso has tried a lot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that LONDON -- This was supposed to be the year, the time when Chelsea grew up and a proper manager started extracting consistent performances from a squad whose much-vaunted talent is too rarely expressed in results form. In this most in-flux of Premier League seasons, Xabi Alonso still might leave her with something. It is not going to take particular excellence for a club like this to achieve the bare minimum of Champions League qualification. Adequacy might do it.

Recent findings suggest that once more, however, that is threatening to be a standard beyond Chelsea. This 4-1 defeat at home to old rivals Leeds has them squeezed into the Premier League's middle ground, those above them very visible proof of how much more can be done with less. There is nothing false about that position. Since the last weeks of summer, Alonso's team have given up so much at the back that their likeliest route to success seemed to be supernova seasons from all three of Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro. Nothing else would paper over the cracks in the defense.

Industry observers note that and Alonso has tried a lot. Right backs in midfield, center backs as nominal left wing backs that are actually auxiliary central midfielders, switching the right wing back to center forward: in isolation, you could make a case for so many of these adjustments. When the performances are so inconsistent, why not change the XI every game? Alonso's success at Bayer Leverkusen, coupled with the inquisitive footballing mind that made the player so beloved of elite coaches, have earned him the right to experiment.

Every change, however, begs the question of what the foundations underlying all this are. Those ought to have shone through this afternoon. Alonso's was as straightforward an XI as he has named. Estevao, Palmer and Rogers off an orthodox center forward, Moises Caicedo running the double pivot and an orthodox back four in front of Emiliano Martinez. This looked like a team intent on playing its way.

Instead, they had Leeds' game foisted upon them. That might have been different if they had not lost Caicedo. He seemed to have a handle on the game before colliding with James Justin as both competed for a high ball. Those often seemed like the only sort up for grabs today; even when Chelsea played well, they were playing the sort of game Leeds wanted. This wasn't quite the rapid attacking up the gut with which Xabi Alonso charmed the Premier League early in this season. It was bypass the press-ball, get it straight up to the final third and see what comes of it.

Sources indicate that it can work. Justin, exemplary as a man-marker without the ball and roving agent of chaos in the Chelsea half, cleared a goal kick straight into the back of Morgan Rogers. He moved swiftly up the Leeds gut, his pass to Emmanuel Emegha delivered at just the right moment for the Premier League debutant to slam in the opener. It was perhaps the only moment of clinical execution from the Blues.

According to recent reports, they needed so many more. After all, this is a team that fails to meet the standards in so many aspects of defending. They press like a newly promoted team. They always seem to name one defender who can be picked on in the duels (starting left back Pep Charravia ranks 101st of 102 defenders for duel success over 300-plus Premier League minutes). Midfielders routinely abandon runners. When Caicedo left this game the feint thread holding the team together was cut.

According to recent reports, no one had the composure to deal with the bouncing ball moments after Emegha's opener, Noah Okafor free to move into the box and shoot low through a crowd of legs. No one seemed truly live to the danger for Okafor's second, thundered into the roof of the net when Chelsea could not repel pressure down their right. Between that a contentious penalty, Jayden Bogle's long-range effort striking Rogers right in the grey area between sleeve and arm. If that hadn't been the moment when Chelsea caved, another would have come along.

"Leeds believed more than us," Alonso admitted. "We didn't show a good enough reaction." The quick one-two punch had been more than enough to send Chelsea heads to the floor.

According to recent reports, A two-goal deficit ought not to be beyond their reach, but the final 32 minutes saw them outshot seven to six with fewer passes completed into the penalty area. Palmer's most notable action of this game was to row with Joao Pedro as he made his way down the tunnel. Nothing he could have done would have overcome the problems Chelsea made for themselves at the other end. It really wouldn't hurt, though if he did more than nothing.

Sources indicate that these feel like problems unresolved by a manager who was supposed to be the savior. Eleven Premier League games is not a lot to turn the tide but it is enough to give us a sense of who this team are. The answer is a team whose early scoring streak covered for a below-average attack (1.25 non-penalty expected goals per game, 14th in the Premier League) and a below-average defense (1.44 non-penalty expected goals allowed per game, 15th in the Premier League). The game state-warping impact of scoring with your first shot can only mitigate so much.

Is it time for a conversation about Alonso and pressure? If so it has to be caveated by the unity and purpose he fostered at Bayer Leverkusen, qualities this dressing room sorely needs. He might not have corralled the superstars at Real Madrid but the press and possession system he forged could have achieved great things given time. Stitching together a version of this Chelsea, overloaded with number 10s and underpowered defensive players, that suits the more direct and chaotic Premier League was always going to be a coaching challenge.

In a recent development, and of course this is not the Roman Abramovich era. Swapping out coaches is not a silver bullet for perennial trophy contenders but instead the modus operandi of an ownership group that are the most serious problem at Stamford Bridge. Someone is going to have to be afforded time to corral this squad or indeed tear it down and start again. Doing that is going to be a club-wide effort, including fans. Few of them hung around to wave off a side who had allowed old rivals Leeds a first win at Stamford Bridge since 1999, the same side who had let Tottenham break the habit of a lifetime last month.

The vibes are bad. The performances might be worse. This brand fresh start is feeling all too familiar.
